title: The winter fat budget
teaches: Torpor, how two grams of fat last a little brown bat the winter, why each waking costs so much, and how white-nose syndrome starves bats
summary: **Torpor is a thermostat turned down.** The bat lets its body fall to a degree or two above the cave's air, and its heart slows from hundreds of beats a minute to ten or twenty.
**A little brown bat has about two grams of fat for the winter.** That is near 80 kilojoules, the energy in three almonds, to last six months.
**A day of torpor costs very little.** About 1.6 mg of fat, so torpor alone would use only a seventh of the store.
**Waking is the expensive part.** Warming from cave temperature to 37 °C and back costs about 108 mg, as much as 68 days of torpor, and wakings take most of the winter's fat.
**Cave temperature sets the cost.** Near freezing the bat must burn fuel to stay above it; warmer caves make torpor dearer; healthy bats choose places near 2 to 7 °C.
**The white-nose fungus grows only in the cold.** *Pseudogymnoascus destructans* thrives on a torpid bat's skin, fastest at 12 to 16 °C, and eats into the wings.
**White-nose kills by waking the bat.** Infected bats wake every few days instead of every few weeks, and run out of fat in late winter.
**The disease crossed a continent in a decade.** First photographed in New York in 2006, it reached Washington in 2016, and some eastern species have lost over 90% of their numbers.

blocks.text: In February 2006 a caver in Howes Cave, a limestone cave in Schoharie County some 50 km west of Albany, New York, photographed a cluster of hibernating little brown bats. Several had a white fuzz on their muzzles, as if they had pushed their faces into icing sugar. Caves are full of moulds, and nobody who saw the pictures that year thought them worth much.

The next winter was different. In January 2007 Al Hicks, the bat specialist of the New York State Department of Environmental Conservation, and his team went into caves near Albany to count the hibernating bats. They found dead bats scattered across the floors, and many of the living ones had the same white noses. That winter bats were also seen flying in daylight over the snow, when there was not an insect in the air.[^hicks]

The dead bats had almost no fat left, at a time of year when a healthy bat still carries a good part of the store it started the winter with. They had starved. The white fuzz turned out to be a fungus growing in the skin of their muzzles and wings. That is this lesson's puzzle: a mould on the skin does not eat an animal's fat, yet these bats were emptied. The answer is in how a small bat gets through a northern winter at all, and it can be worked out with a little arithmetic.

All the chemical work a body does to stay alive, pumping blood, repairing itself and above all making heat, is its **metabolism**. It runs on fuel: sugar for quick use, fat for storage. Energy is counted in joules; a kilojoule (kJ), a thousand joules, is about the energy it takes to lift a 1 kg bag of sugar 100 metres. A gram of fat holds about 39 kJ, more than twice as much as a gram of sugar, which is why animals store fat for lean times.[^calories]

A little brown bat weighs about 8 g. A body that small has a great deal of skin for its bulk and loses heat fast. In winter there are no flying insects in New York or Washington State for five or six months. Kept at 37 °C in a cave a few degrees above freezing, a bat that size would burn something like half a gram of fat a day, a rough estimate, and get through its whole winter store in a few days.

So it lets itself go cold. In **torpor** a bat turns down the set point of its internal thermostat, the temperature its body defends, until its body sits a degree or two above the air around it. Its heart slows from a few hundred beats a minute to ten or twenty, it breathes in short bursts with long pauses between them, and its metabolism falls to a few per cent of what it uses awake and resting. Torpor is not sleep. A sleeping animal stays warm and its brain runs through the stages of sleep; a torpid bat is cold, slow and hard to rouse. It is still under control, though. If the cave nears freezing, a torpid bat burns a little more fuel to stay above it, or wakes and moves somewhere better.

blocks.caption: A little brown bat awake at rest and in torpor in a 5 °C cave: body temperature, ten seconds of heartbeats (each tick is one beat), and the energy it uses. Round numbers; the heart of a torpid bat also stops for seconds at a time.

blocks.text: **Hibernation** is a winter of torpor taken in long bouts, each lasting from days to a few weeks, separated by short wakings. Many bats of the northern United States and Canada hibernate in caves and old mines, where the temperature stays nearly steady all winter. Others, such as the hoary bat, migrate south instead, as lesson 10, The way home, follows.

parts.title: Two grams for half a year

blocks.text: A little brown bat goes into hibernation in October with about 2 g of fat under its skin and around its organs, gathered by eating hard through late summer and autumn. At 39 kJ a gram that is near 80 kJ, the energy in about three almonds. It has to last until mid April: some 180 to 200 days.

In 1990 Donald Thomas, a bat biologist at the University of Sherbrooke in Quebec, and his students Michel Dorais and Jean-Marie Bergeron worked out the budget. They measured how much oxygen little brown bats used while torpid and through each waking, and turned it into milligrams of fat.[^thomas] A day of torpor near 5 °C used about 1.6 mg. Over 190 days that is about 300 mg, a seventh of the store. Torpor alone would leave a healthy bat plump in spring.

The rest goes on the wakings. Every two or three weeks a hibernating bat rouses. It shivers and burns a special heat-making fat between its shoulders, warming itself from the cave's temperature to 37 °C in under an hour; it stays warm for an hour or more, perhaps drinking or moving to a new spot; then it cools down again. Nobody is sure why bats wake at all.[^why] Before the next figure shows the answer, guess what one waking costs.

blocks.caption: The fat a little brown bat burns, in milligrams, after Thomas, Dorais and Bergeron (1990), on a ratio scale: equal distances along the bar mean equal multiples, so the stretch from 1 to 10 mg is as long as the stretch from 10 to 100 mg.
blocks.task: Guess the cost of one waking

items.label: One waking
items.says: about 108 mg, as much as 68 days of torpor

guess.ask: A day of torpor burns about 1.6 mg of fat. How much does one waking burn?

blocks.text: One waking costs about 108 mg, as much fat as 68 days of torpor. Warming the whole body by more than 30 degrees and holding it there in a cold cave is expensive, and torpor is so cheap that any time spent warm dwarfs it.

blocks.title: An estimate
points: A healthy bat wakes about every two weeks: some 13 wakings in a 190-day winter. Thirteen wakings at 108 mg is about 1.4 g, and torpor adds 0.3 g, so the bat ends the winter with 0.3 g to spare. More than four fifths of what it burned went on the wakings. Two extra wakings a month, and the store runs out before spring.

parts.title: A fungus that likes the cold

blocks.text: The white fuzz is *Pseudogymnoascus destructans*, a fungus first described in 2009.[^name] Like other fungi (the Fungi course on this site covers them), it grows as a web of fine threads that feed by digesting what they grow into. Unusually, it grows only in the cold: from about 3 °C upward, fastest between about 12 and 16 °C, and not at all above about 20 °C. On an active bat at 37 °C it cannot grow. A torpid bat, cooled to the temperature of its cave, is an ideal place for it.

The disease it causes is called **white-nose syndrome** after the fuzz on the muzzle, but the damage that matters is on the [[wings|wing]]. A bat's wing is a thin double layer of living skin stretched between the fingers, as lesson 2 showed, and it makes up most of the bat's surface. It carries blood vessels close under the surface, helps control how much water the bat loses, and takes some part in exchanging gases. The fungus eats into this skin, leaving small cup-shaped pits packed with its threads.

In 2012 DeeAnn Reeder of Bucknell University and her colleagues fitted hibernating bats with small temperature loggers and recorded every waking. Healthy little brown bats woke every two weeks or so. Bats with white-nose woke every three or four days by late winter, and the ones that woke most often died first. Why the fungus wakes them is still argued. The leading idea is that damaged wings lose water, and the bats wake to drink; another is that the body wakes to react to the infection. Either way, each waking costs its 108 mg.[^cryan] Infected bats also burn fat somewhat faster while torpid, but the extra wakings are by far the bigger drain. The fungus does not eat the bat's fat; it makes the bat spend it.

The figure below runs a winter for one little brown bat with the numbers above. The fat gauge falls slowly through each bout of torpor and drops a step at each waking; the strip on top shows the body temperature, with a spike to 37 °C for each waking. The Date slider plays the winter as a time lapse.

blocks.caption: A little brown bat's fat from 15 October to late April. Torpor and waking costs after Thomas, Dorais and Bergeron (1990); with white-nose, the time between wakings shrinks toward three and a half days as the fungus spreads, faster in warmer caves. A model: the fungus's growth curve is simplified and set so a 7 °C cave matches what was seen in New York.
blocks.task: Guess when the fat runs out, then give the bat white-nose

blocks.text: Without the fungus, the bat comes through. Move the cave's temperature and the cost of torpor follows it: warmer caves make every day dearer, and below about 2 °C the bat has to burn fuel to keep its tissues from freezing. Healthy bats pick the parts of a cave between about 2 and 7 °C, which is why hibernating bats cluster in particular spots, often deep inside or near cold air flowing in. Move the healthy waking interval and the budget swings much more: wakings are what decide how much is left.

With white-nose, the wakings come faster and faster as the fungus spreads, and in a 7 °C cave the fat runs out in February. In a warmer cave the fungus grows faster and the bat dies sooner. In a cave near 3 °C it barely grows at all. In 2012 Kate Langwig and her colleagues, comparing the declines at many hibernation sites in the northeast, found the same in real caves: colonies in colder, drier sites declined less than those in warmer, wetter ones. A bat that has run out of fat in February does the only thing left, and flies out to look for food. Those were the bats seen over the snow near Albany.

The fungus was soon found on bats across Europe, from France to Ukraine, where it grows on hibernating bats without killing them in large numbers. European bats seem to have lived with it for a very long time, and it most likely came to New York from Europe, perhaps on a caver's boots or clothing, though no one knows how. In North America it met bats that had never faced it.

blocks.caption: White-nose syndrome in North America, from the first photograph to the West.

events.label: White noses photographed in Howes Cave, New York
events.text: A caver photographs hibernating little brown bats with white fuzz on their muzzles, west of Albany.

events.label: Dead bats in caves near Albany
events.text: Al Hicks's team finds dead bats in caves near Albany, and bats are seen flying in daylight in midwinter.

events.label: Vermont, Massachusetts, Connecticut
events.text: The disease spreads into New England, carried mostly by bats meeting at caves in autumn.

events.label: The fungus named; four more states
events.text: The fungus is described and named; white-nose reaches New Hampshire, New Jersey, Pennsylvania and West Virginia.

events.label: Canada; the same fungus in Europe
events.text: White-nose reaches Ontario and Quebec. The same fungus is found on bats across Europe, which are not dying of it.

events.label: 5.7 to 6.7 million bats dead
events.text: Wildlife agencies estimate that between 5.7 and 6.7 million bats have died in eastern North America.

events.label: A little brown bat near North Bend, Washington
events.text: Hikers find a sick bat near North Bend, about 50 km east of Seattle, some 2,100 km (1,300 miles) beyond the nearest known case. It dies two days later.

events.label: More than 40 states
events.text: White-nose has been confirmed in 41 states and in several Canadian provinces.

blocks.text: The losses are among the worst for any wild mammals in North America. Millions of bats have died, and in the east the little brown bat, the northern long-eared bat and the tricolored bat have each lost more than 90% of their numbers. The northern long-eared bat is now listed as endangered in the United States.

On 11 March 2016 hikers near North Bend, on the edge of the Cascades in King County, picked up a little brown bat that could barely fly and took it to a wildlife shelter, where it died two days later. Tests at the US Geological Survey's wildlife health laboratory found white-nose syndrome, the first case in western North America, about 1,300 miles (2,100 km) from the nearest known case in Nebraska. The fungus on it matched the eastern strain, which suggests a long jump, possibly with human help, rather than slow spread across the plains.[^jump] It has since been found widely in western Washington, on the Yuma myotis, a small bat that feeds low over water, as well as on little brown bats. Both belong to *Myotis*, the mouse-eared bats, a group of several dozen small insect-eating species.

There is a little good news. In parts of the east some little brown bat colonies, after the crash, have held steady at a small fraction of their old size, and the survivors may be bats that store more fat or choose colder roosts. Whether they can rebuild is the subject of the next lesson. Meanwhile cavers clean their gear between caves, many caves are closed in winter, and Washington's wildlife department asks people to report sick or dead bats, especially in winter.

blocks.caption: Five questions on the winter budget
blocks.task: Choose the best answer to each

items.ask: What is a hibernating bat doing when it is in torpor?
choices: Holding its body a degree or two above the cave's air, with its heart and metabolism slowed to a few per cent
Sleeping deeply at its normal body temperature, with its breathing slowed
Cooling to whatever the cave's temperature is, with no control over it at all
items.why: Torpor is a lowered set point, not sleep and not passive cooling: the bat stays cold to save fuel, but still burns extra to stay above freezing and can wake when it must.

items.ask: A hibernating little brown bat burns about 1.6 mg of fat a day in torpor and about 108 mg for each waking. Waking every two weeks, where does most of the fat it burns over the winter go?
choices: On the wakings, which take more than four fifths of it
On the days of torpor, because there are so many of them
About evenly between torpor and the wakings
items.why: Waking every two weeks gives about 13 wakings in a 190-day winter: about 1.4 g at 108 mg each, against about 0.3 g for 190 days of torpor at 1.6 mg. One waking costs as much as 68 days of torpor.

items.ask: Which explanation of how white-nose syndrome kills bats fits the evidence best?
choices: The fungus makes the bats wake far more often, and the extra wakings use up their fat
The fungus digests the bat's stored fat directly from under the skin
The fungus blocks the bat's nose so it cannot breathe in torpor
items.why: Infected bats wake every three or four days instead of every two weeks or so. At about 108 mg a waking, the store is gone by late winter.

items.ask: Two caves hold little brown bats infected with the white-nose fungus. One stays at 4 °C, the other at 10 °C. What would you predict?
choices: The bats in the warmer cave run out of fat sooner, because the fungus grows faster and torpor costs more there
The bats in the colder cave run out sooner, because they must burn fuel to keep warm
Both run out at the same time, because the fungus wakes them equally often
items.why: The fungus grows faster the warmer the cave, from 3 °C up to its best at 12 to 16 °C, and torpor is dearer in warmer air. Colonies in colder sites have declined less.

items.ask: Why were bats seen flying in daylight over snow in a New York winter?
choices: They had run out of fat and were flying out to look for food that winter could not give them
Warm days had woken them early and they were moving to a new cave
The fungus makes bats see daylight as dusk
items.why: A starving bat at the end of its fat has nothing left to burn in torpor, so it flies out. There are no flying insects in February, and many were found dead on the snow.

hicks.title: Al Hicks
hicks.text: Alan Hicks led bat work for New York's Department of Environmental Conservation for many years and was one of the first to raise the alarm. The caver's photograph from Howes Cave, taken the winter before, is the earliest known record of the disease in North America.

calories.title: Kilojoules and calories
calories.text: Food labels count energy in kilocalories, the 'Calories' of a diet. One kilocalorie is 4.184 kJ, so a gram of fat holds about 9 kilocalories and the bat's 2 g about 19.

thomas.title: Fat from oxygen
thomas.text: Burning a gram of fat in the body takes about two litres of oxygen. Thomas and his students kept bats in sealed chambers at cave temperatures and measured the oxygen they used, in torpor and through a whole waking, warming, staying warm and cooling down again. The figures in their paper, published in the Journal of Mammalogy in 1990, are the ones used in this lesson.

why.title: Why wake at all?
why.text: If wakings cost so much, a bat that never woke would save most of its fat. Something must need doing. Ideas include drinking, since a torpid bat slowly loses water through its skin; getting rid of waste; letting the immune system, which hardly works in the cold, catch up; and making up some kind of sleep, which a torpid brain may not get. The evidence for each is mixed.

name.title: Two names
name.text: The fungus was first named *Geomyces destructans* in 2009. When its family tree was studied more closely it was moved, in 2013, to the genus *Pseudogymnoascus*, so older papers use the first name.

cryan.title: Water and wings
cryan.text: Paul Cryan of the US Geological Survey and colleagues proposed in 2010 that the damage to the wing disturbs the bat's control of water and salts. Later studies found infected bats lose more water by evaporation and burn fat faster even while torpid, which fits that idea.

jump.title: A long jump
jump.text: Bats do not normally travel from the Midwest to the Cascades. Genetic studies of the fungus from Washington found it closest to strains from the eastern United States, which is why people moving between caves, or goods moving across the country, are suspected, though the route has never been traced.
